newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid agencies to send convoy for lost Zaireans.
newsitem.headline: Aid agencies to send convoy for lost Zaireans.

text.p: Two aid agencies said on Monday they were sending trucks into remote areas of eastern Zaire to help tens of thousands of Hutu refugees and Zairean civilians who fled west to escape a Tutsi-led revolt.

The U.N. Children's Fund and Medecins Sans Frontieres said they were sending a joint convoy of five trucks under military escort with 40 tonnes of food and medicines down the road from Kisangani towards Walikale, 350 km (220 miles) away.

"We don't know exactly where the displaced people are, but it appears there is a big concentration at Masisi, at Walikale and at Shabunda (180 km west of Bukavu) where priests tell us there are more than 40,000 people," Eric Mercier of UNICEF told a news conference in the Zaire capital.

An estimated 500,000 Rwandan Hutus have returned home since Friday, after an alliance of Tutsi and other rebels opposed to absent and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko attacked the refugee camps where they had lived for over two years.
Mercier said that as yet there was no idea of where far more Rwandan and Burundian refugees and Zairean civilians had fled.
Insecurity brought by troops retreating from the eastern warfront and living off the land have hampered operations.
"We expect to help the military, it's a matter of realism, it's not something we usually do but without helping the military there will be no access to civilians," Mercier said.
Earlier, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said it was launching an operation in eastern Zaire to search for Hutu refugees and displaced Zairean civilians.

"Hundreds of thousands of refugees have returned to Rwanda, but we must not forget that there are still hundreds of thousands missing, as well as displaced Zaireans," ICRC spokesman Josue Anselmo told Reuters.

Anselmo said a Zairean Red Cross worker who had walked 350 km (220 miles) in 17 days from the now rebel-held eastern town of Bukavu before finding a vehicle to the city of Kisangani had said thousands of people were left behind.
"All the way along he was passing women with babies, there was never five minutes when he walked without seeing another group," he said.

The ICRC has opened an office in Kisangani and hopes to distribute aid once the displaced and refugees are found. "If they are scattered it is better in some ways because they will be able to live from local villages. If they are concentrated then there is a very real risk of disease," Anselmo said.
So far only the Roman Catholic Church and the Kisangani business association have tried to send trucks into the tens of thousands of square kilometres which may conceal the displaced.
